Japan's Nikkei Stock Average Rebounds on Semiconductor Rally; Up 997 Yen at Morning Close to 61,816
sum: On the morning of the 13th, the Nikkei Stock Average rebounded on the Tokyo stock market, closing the morning session at 61,816.72, up 997.36 yen from the previous day. Buying spread across a wide range of sectors, led by semiconductor-related stocks that had fallen the previous day, and the gain briefly exceeded 1,000 yen. The Tokyo Stock Price Index (TOPIX) ended morning trading up 30.21 points at 3,967.54.

The market opened higher at 61,223.41, up 404.05 yen from the previous day. Buying continued thereafter, and by 10:15 a.m. the index had risen more than 900 yen at one point. Advantest (6857.T) alone lifted the Nikkei by roughly 300 yen, while non-semiconductor names such as Fast Retailing (9983.T) and Recruit Holdings (6098.T) were also firm.

On the Prime Market, gainers accounted for about 60% of all issues, while decliners were limited to 28%. Volume was 1,078.14 million shares, and turnover was ¥3.8653 trillion (approximately $24.2 billion). Among the 33 sector indices, services, other products and retail rose, while precision instruments, air transport and mining fell. The Standard TOP20, Growth 250 and Growth Core indices all rebounded as well.

In afternoon trading, selling on the rebound in high-priced semiconductor-related stocks weighed on the upside. The afternoon session opened at 61,576.67, up 757.31 yen from the previous day. Profit-taking emerged in some semiconductor-related names, trimming the gain from the morning close. Market participants noted that while short-term bargain-hunting buying centered on tech stocks is coming in, selling is also quick. They said buying driven by a sense of bargains following the previous week's sharp decline is spreading across a wide range of issues, and Toyota Motor (7203.T) turned positive in the afternoon.

In the U.S. market the previous day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell back, and the Nasdaq Composite was also weak. In the foreign exchange market, the yen declined, briefly touching the 160-per-dollar level for the first time in about two months.
Note: Figures are as of the end of morning trading on the 13th.
With investor sentiment chilled by the previous week's sharp slump, buybacks originating in semiconductor-related shares lifted the overall market.

Nikkei Stock Average Opens Higher for Fourth Straight Session, Buyers Shrug Off Report of NVIDIA CEO's Removal
sum: On the Tokyo stock market on the 12th, the Nikkei Stock Average opened higher for a fourth consecutive session. It opened at 61,475.11, above the previous day's close of 61,248 (up 226.52 from the previous day), and has since widened its gains slightly. Carrying over the prior day's buying of AI-related shares in the U.S. market, semiconductor-related names led the advance.

In the prior day's U.S. stock market, the Nasdaq Composite rebounded, rising more than 1.5%. AI cloud provider CoreWeave's quarterly earnings, which showed a strong demand outlook, temporarily eased concerns about the sustainability of AI-related capital investment. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), composed of semiconductor-related stocks, also rose more than 5%, and in the Tokyo market, buying was dominant in AI and semiconductor-related names such as Tokyo Electron.

Still, the advance was not one-sided. Although the Nikkei at one point rose more than 400 points, investor sentiment cooled when reports emerged concerning the removal of NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang, and the index fell nearly 200 points at one stage. The electronic edition of the U.S. newspaper Wall Street Journal reported on the morning of the 12th Japan time that NVIDIA's board is preparing to remove Huang, amid an extramarital affair scandal involving a woman suspected of being a Chinese government spy. NVIDIA's share price plunged in after-hours trading, and U.S. stock index futures also fell on the morning of the 12th Japan time.

According to market participants, given that futures had been bought up to 62,020 in overnight trading on the Osaka Exchange, the opening gain was limited. Caution over the removal report appeared to cap the upside.

By sector, oil products, real estate, other products, and marine transportation posted relatively large gains. Buying spread across a broad range of sectors, and the Tokyo Stock Exchange's TOPIX also extended its gains. The yen's depreciation to the upper 159 range per dollar also supported export-related shares. Among individual stocks, SoftBank Group (9984.T), Shin-Etsu Chemical (4063.T), and Fast Retailing (9983.T) were higher, while Advantest (6857.T), Recruit Holdings (6098.T), and Ibiden (4062.T) were lower.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average briefly climbs more than 500 points as AI investment fears ease and earnings-driven buying supports market
sum: In the morning session on the 11th, the Nikkei Stock Average traded firmly in the Tokyo stock market, with scenes of it rising more than 500 points from the previous day. Following last week's roughly 6,000-point decline, bargain-hunting focused on strong corporate earnings is flowing in as a rebound.

As of 10:20 a.m., the Nikkei had widened its gain to around 60,900, up about 450 points from the previous day. On the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market, more than half of the stocks were advancing, with trading value reaching an estimated ¥2.3184 trillion (approximately $14.6 billion) and trading volume reaching 720.9 million shares. Market participants noted, "There is a strong view that last week's decline was excessive, and this week the market has entered a rebound phase."

One of the main factors pushing the market higher was that U.S. emerging AI cloud company CoreWeave's revenue for the July-September 2026 quarter exceeded market expectations. Concerns that had been smoldering recently about the sustainability of AI infrastructure investment eased, and semiconductor-related stocks such as Advantest (6857.T) and Tokyo Electron (8035.T) rebounded from morning declines. An official at a major securities firm said, "Anxiety that AI-related capital investment will run out of steam has receded, and buying is returning to high-priced stocks."

Among individual stocks, Kioxia rose, apparently as the unwinding of margin-trading long positions progressed. Fast Retailing, TDK, Lasertec, and Sumitomo Realty & Development were also higher. On the other hand, Konami Group, Recruit, BayCurrent, and Suzuki were lower. Financial stocks were also solid on rising interest rates.

Following the previous day's decline in major U.S. stock indexes, selling emerged in some high-priced AI and semiconductor stocks immediately after the open. The Nikkei started with a modest gain of ¥65.72 at 60,525.30, up from the previous trading day, and trading was mixed.

SoftBank Group (9984.T), which drew attention, opened at a sell quote after announcing a loss-making interim earnings report after the close of the Tokyo market on the 10th. It briefly fell more than 10% but then pared losses and became a support for the overall market.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average Briefly Reclaims 60,000 Level as U.S. AI Shares Rally, Oil Slump Provide Support
sum: Japan's Nikkei Stock Average extended sharp gains on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on Nov. 10, briefly reclaiming the 60,000 level during trading hours. Carrying over the prior day's buyback of AI (artificial intelligence) and semiconductor-related shares in the U.S. market, broad-based buying centered on chip stocks emerged. A sharp drop in crude oil futures also contributed to improved investor sentiment.

The morning session closed at 60,475.78, up 1,700.28 points, or 2.89%, from the previous trading day. After widening its gain to 1,843.95 points (3.14%) to hit a high of 60,619.45 shortly after the open, the index gave up some ground on selling into strength and traded in a range near its highs. The TOPIX ended the morning session up 2.22% at 3,902.85.

This is the first time in two trading days, since Friday, Nov. 6, that the Nikkei has topped 60,000. Last week, following a landslide victory by the Democratic Party in the U.S. midterm elections held Nov. 3, selling swelled on concerns over tighter AI regulation, including curbs on data center construction in the United States, and the Nikkei fell by more than 5,800 points over the week. In addition to a rebound from the sharp decline, the recovery in high-tech shares in the U.S. market on Nov. 9 prompted buybacks in Tokyo.

In the U.S. market the prior day, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rebounded sharply for the first time in three sessions, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), composed of major chip stocks, rose nearly 7%. In Tokyo, Advantest (6857.T) posted sharp gains, while Kioxia Holdings (285A.T) and SoftBank Group (9984.T) traded firmly. Mitsubishi UFJ Financial Group (8306.T) and Fast Retailing (9983.T) were also bought.

By sector, 26 of 33 sectors advanced, with nonferrous metals, banks, electric appliances, and glass and ceramic products among the top gainers. Meanwhile, other financial services, food products, and land transportation declined. On the TSE Prime Market, the number of advancing issues reached 1,209 (77%), while decliners totaled just 322 (20%). Trading value was a brisk ¥4.206915 trillion (approximately $26.6 billion).
Another factor lifting the market was the oil slump.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average Rebounds After 6 Sessions, Up 1,340 Points to 58,775 on Semiconductor Stock Buybacks
sum: On Nov. 9, the Nikkei Stock Average rebounded for the first time in six sessions on the Tokyo stock market, closing at 58,775.50, up 1,340.73 points (2.33%) from the end of the previous week. Carrying over the buyback of high-tech and semiconductor-related stocks in the U.S. market late last week, buying in Tokyo also led with a broad range of issues, centering on artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor-related names. However, after buying ran its course, selling on rebounds capped the upside, and many see the move as within the scope of a technical rebound.

The Nikkei opened at 57,960.70, up 525.93 points, and the advance briefly exceeded 2,000 points to reach 59,440. After ending morning trading at 59,411.34, up 1,976.57 points (3.44%) from the end of the previous week, the index trimmed its gains in the afternoon. On the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market, advancing issues totaled 1,415 (91%), amounting to gains across nearly the entire market, while decliners were limited to 123 issues (7%). Trading value was ¥8.911842 trillion (approximately $56.4 billion), and volume was 2.99581 billion shares.

On the Tokyo market on Friday, Nov. 6, stocks fell across the board amid concerns over a slowdown in AI-related investment and tighter data center regulations after Democrats won the U.S. midterm elections, with the Nikkei's decline exceeding 3,600 points — the third-largest closing drop on record. The rebound on Nov. 9 was a reaction to that selloff.

By sector, 31 of the 33 Tokyo Stock Exchange sectors rose, with only foods and marine transportation declining. The top gainers by percentage included nonferrous metals, banking, other products, oil and coal products, and electric appliances. Among individual stocks, high-priced AI-related names such as Tokyo Electron (8035.T) and Advantest (6857.T) were bought, and Fast Retailing (9983.T) was the top positive contributor to the Nikkei. Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (7011.T), Furukawa Electric (5801.T), and Minebea Mitsumi (6479.T) were also firm.
Meanwhile, some AI-related names showed a sluggish rebound. Kioxia Holdings (285A.T) and SoftBank Group (9984.T) moved weakly.

Nikkei Plunges as Much as 4,300 Points, Briefly Falls Below ¥60,000; AI Regulation Fears Hit Chip Stocks
sum: The Nikkei Stock Average plunged on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on Nov. 6, closing down 3,643.13 points, or 5.96%, at 57,434.77. The intraday decline at one point exceeded 4,300 points, and the benchmark briefly fell below the ¥60,000 threshold for the first time in about five and a half months. The closing drop was the third-largest on record. Following a broad selloff in artificial intelligence and semiconductor-related stocks in the U.S. market the previous day, selling surged in related issues in Tokyo as well. On the Tokyo Stock Exchange's Prime Market, 98% of issues declined, resulting in an across-the-board rout.

The trigger was the U.S. stock market on Nov. 5. After the Democratic Party—viewed as favorable toward AI regulation—secured majorities in both chambers of Congress in the U.S. midterm elections, expectations spread rapidly that headwinds would strengthen for data center construction and AI development. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1,833.06 points, or 3.44%, to close at 51,523.06. Nvidia, the symbol of the AI boom, dropped 9.2%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite also tumbled, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX Index) recorded a decline of more than 12%.

The Tokyo market took the full brunt of that move. The Nikkei opened down 703.55 points at 60,374.35. It then accelerated its decline, falling below 57,000 at one point during mid-morning trading, with the drop exceeding 4,300 points. SoftBank Group (9984.T), which carries heavy weight in the index, fell ¥431 to ¥3,549; Advantest (6857.T) dropped ¥1,470 to ¥28,015; and Tokyo Electron (8035.T) fell ¥490 to ¥8,263. These three stocks alone pushed the Nikkei down by roughly 1,500 points. Kioxia Holdings (285A.T) fell 8%, while Fast Retailing (9983.T) and Recruit Holdings (6098.T) also posted sharp declines.
Note: Closing prices as of the Nov. 6 close. Trading value on the Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market was ¥12.4808 trillion (approximately $78.9 billion), and trading volume was 4.30583 billion shares.
By sector, all 33 industry groups on the Tokyo Stock Exchange declined, with no sector advancing. The steepest declines were in foods, oil and coal products, and real estate.

Japan's Nikkei 225 Begins Rebound as U.S. Stock Gains and Oil Price Plunge Offer Support, but AI and Semiconductor Shares Weigh
sum: The Nikkei 225 began trading higher on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on November 5, opening at 62,384.73 yen, up 196.10 yen (0.32%) from the previous trading day. Buying led the market, carrying over the momentum from gains in all three major U.S. stock indexes the prior day.

Two factors pushed the market up. One was the firm performance of the U.S. stock market as it digested the results of the U.S. midterm elections. The other was a sharp drop in crude oil prices as views spread that tensions in the Middle East were easing. Lower energy costs support investor sentiment through both corporate earnings and household burdens.
Among blue-chip shares, Toyota Motor (7203.T) surged, while Sony Group (6758.T) and index-heavyweight Fast Retailing (9983.T) were quoted higher.

On the other hand, artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor-related shares saw notable declines. SoftBank Group (9984.T), Tokyo Electron (8035.T), and Advantest (6857.T) all fell sharply, as caution over the direction of AI regulation continued to simmer.

In the previous day's trading on November 4, these three semiconductor and AI-related stocks alone pushed the Nikkei 225 down by about 1,241 yen at one point. Selling tends to concentrate in stocks with large index weightings, and this structure continues to amplify swings across the broader market.

Among market participants, the near-term focus is whether buybacks will emerge in the sharply fallen semiconductor shares. On the previous day, some stocks such as Fast Retailing and Nintendo (7974.T) rose, so the market was not uniformly lower. Some see the fact that buying interest is not one-sided as a sign of the market's underlying resilience.

On the overseas front, reports on vote counting in the U.S. midterm elections were also coming in during Tokyo trading hours, and market participants are focused on how U.S. long-term interest rates and foreign exchange rates react. Domestically, earnings announcements from companies such as IHI (7013.T), Mitsubishi Corp (8058.T), and NTT (9432.T) are scheduled during trading hours, and stock price reactions to individual earnings results could divide winners and losers within sectors.

sum: The Nikkei share average fell 3.56% to 60,835.36 by the midday break, hitting its lowest level since July 29, while the broader Topix slipped 2.45% to 3,832.27.

Democrats flipped a Republican-held Senate seat in North Carolina and performed strongly in several Republican-leaning House districts in Florida, raising hopes they could regain control of Congress.

In Japan, shares of chip-testing equipment maker Advantest and Tokyo Electron fell 7.8% and 6.28%, respectively, while technology investor SoftBank Group slipped roughly 9%. Memory chip maker Kioxia was down 11.55%.

Japanese tech shares, but strong earnings and outlooks from companies such as Advantest and Tokyo Electron should help underpin valuations, said Kazuaki Shimada, chief strategist at IwaiCosmo Securities.

Mukesh Ambani gains $8.5 billion in a day to become Asia’s richest person: What triggered the surge?
sum: Mukesh Ambani became Asia's richest person after his estimated wealth rose by $8.5 billion in a single day. A sharp rally in Reliance Industries shares, supported by strong quarterly earnings, pushed his fortune to approximately $88.8 billion and lifted him above other leading Asian billionaires.

Reliance Industries chairman Mukesh Ambani became Asia’s richest person on Monday, November 2, 2026, after his estimated wealth jumped by $8.5 billion in a single trading session. According to Forbes’ Real-Time Billionaires List, Ambani’s fortune rose to $88.8 billion, placing him 23rd among the world’s richest people. The sudden increase came after Reliance Industries shares recorded their biggest single-day rally in more than six years.

The rally added approximately ₹1.84 lakh crore to Reliance Industries’ market value, taking it to around ₹17.6 lakh crore. Ambani’s wealth is closely linked to his shareholding in the company, which explains why a sharp rise in its stock price can add billions to his estimated fortune within hours. The increase represents the higher market value of his investments rather than money deposited into his bank account.

The biggest trigger was Reliance Industries’ September-quarter financial performance. The company reported a 40.6 percent increase in consolidated net profit to ₹25,548 crore, beating market expectations.
Reliance shares surged 11.6 percent on Monday to close at around ₹1,300.
- Oil business: Better refining and petrochemical margins supported higher earnings.
- Investor confidence: Better-than-expected results encouraged buying in Reliance shares, even as its retail business continued to face profitability pressures.

items.t: Fast Retailing (TSE:9983) Stock May Be Overvalued Following Raised FY2027 Forecast
sum: Fast Retailing has been on a powerful multi year run, and the question investors keep circling back to is whether the current share price is still anchored to what the business earns. With the spotlight now firmly on its earnings profile, the issue is how much of that past success is already built into today's valuation.
- Over the past 5 years the stock has returned 210.2%, which puts real pressure on investors to judge whether the present earnings base can shoulder that kind of optimism.

- Management has raised its longer term forecast on the back of Uniqlo's outperformance, which can support expectations for stronger earnings power if execution stays on track and structural reforms in other units pay off.
- The analysts covering Fast Retailing have run their own numbers. See what analysts think Fast Retailing's shares could be worth.
The stock's next move may depend on whether Fast Retailing's current earnings are strong enough to justify the price investors are being asked to pay today.
If you want to stress test this same earnings driven valuation question beyond Fast Retailing, compare it with companies in the 12 high quality undervalued stocks

The P/E ratio is a useful starting point for Fast Retailing because investors are squarely focused on what the business currently earns per share. On this measure, the stock trades on around 40.6x earnings, which is well above the Specialty Retail industry average of about 12.8x and also higher than the peer group near 17.3x. That kind of premium means the market is attaching a much richer price tag to each yen of Fast Retailing earnings than to many other retailers.

Fast Retailing FY2026 annual earnings: record profit for 5th year
sum: Fast Retailing reported its fifth consecutive year of record profit on Thursday, as Uniqlo sales rose across every region and new store openings in the United States and Europe drove growth beyond its traditional Japanese and Chinese markets.
Net profit for the fiscal year ended August 31 rose 25% to 542.52 billion yen. Annual revenue grew 17% to 3.9633 trillion yen, and business profit climbed 30% to 718.4 billion yen, the company said.
The results beat analyst expectations. A consensus of analysts polled by data provider Visible Alpha had projected net profit of 510.7 billion yen, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Fast Retailing's international Uniqlo operations were the standout performer, with revenue rising 26% to 2.4111 trillion yen and business profit expanding 44% to 439.8 billion yen. North America posted a 35% revenue gain to 364.9 billion yen and a 53% jump in business profit, while Europe's revenue rose 39% to 512.6 billion yen and its business profit expanded 69% to 91.7 billion yen. For the first time, combined sales from North America and Europe exceeded those from Greater China and also surpassed those from South Korea and the Southeast Asia, India and Australia region, the company said.
North America contributed 9.2% of total company revenue during the fiscal year, with Europe at 13%. Greater China — encompassing Hong Kong and Taiwan — represented 18%.

In Greater China, where profit fell the previous year amid weak consumer demand, business profit rose 25% to 112.0 billion yen. The company said it plans to reopen its flagship Uniqlo store in Shanghai on October 30.

Chief Executive Tadashi Yanai said that Uniqlo's rising profile in the U.S. and Europe is pulling in shoppers from elsewhere, pointing specifically to Southeast Asia, India and Australia, according to the Wall Street Journal. "This is a big chance to realize further growth," Yanai said, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Nikkei Nears 70,000 as AI Shares Rally on Fed Pause Hopes
sum: TOKYO - Tokyo stocks surged on October 5, with the Nikkei 225 closing at 69,947, up 1,637 points, after briefly recovering the 70,000 level for the first time in about three months, as weak U.S. jobs data reduced expectations for an October Federal Reserve rate hike and buying spread through artificial intelligence and semiconductor-related shares.

The broader TOPIX rose 54.22 points to 4,145.22, showing that the rally was not limited to the price-weighted Nikkei. However, the day’s strongest momentum was concentrated in AI, semiconductor, electronic-component and high-priced growth names, which have again become the main drivers of Tokyo’s market.

The Nikkei opened sharply higher and quickly moved into a powerful risk-on pattern. During the morning session, the index briefly rose above 70,000, recovering that level during trading hours for the first time in about three months. Profit-taking emerged later, but the index still closed just below 70,000 at 69,947.

The rally followed the release of weaker-than-expected U.S. employment data at the end of last week. The slowdown in U.S. job growth led investors to scale back expectations that the Federal Reserve will raise rates again at its October meeting, easing pressure on global growth shares.

The shift in Fed expectations gave investors a reason to return to AI and semiconductor shares. These stocks are sensitive to interest rates because much of their valuation depends on future earnings growth. When rate-hike expectations fall, investors become more willing to buy high-growth technology names.

The U.S. market provided the first push. American technology shares rose after the jobs data, and that momentum carried into Tokyo. Semiconductor, AI and electronic-component shares drew heavy buying from the opening bell.

Tokyo Electron, Advantest, SoftBank Group, TDK and other AI-linked names were central to the advance. Investors bought companies tied to advanced chipmaking equipment, chip testing, electronic components, data-center infrastructure and AI platforms.

Japan's Nikkei Stock Average extends sharp gains, briefly surges 1,600 yen on concentrated AI-related buying
sum: The Nikkei Stock Average extended sharp gains in the morning session on October 1 on the Tokyo Stock Exchange. The morning close stood at 68,355.81, up 1,602.09 points (2.40%) from the previous day. Strong earnings from U.S. semiconductor giant Micron Technology fueled concentrated buying in artificial intelligence (AI)-related names, lifting the index. The TOPIX, by contrast, rose only 5.32 points to 4,113.97, with profit-taking pressure evident across the broader market.

Micron announced on September 30 (U.S. time) its fiscal 2026 fourth-quarter (June–August) results, with revenue reaching $54.229 billion — roughly 4.8 times the year-earlier level — exceeding market expectations of $51.07 billion. GAAP earnings per share came to $32.87, compared with $2.83 a year earlier. The company guided for revenue of approximately $61.5 billion in the September–November quarter, signaling that AI demand remains robust.

In the morning session, advancing issues numbered 512 versus 991 decliners and 40 unchanged, with decliners far outnumbering advancers. While more than 60% of Tokyo Stock Exchange Prime Market stocks fell, buying in a select group of high-priced semiconductor-related names underpinned the Nikkei average.

The largest positive contributor to the Nikkei average was Advantest (6857.T), adding 648.05 points to the index. Its shares ended the morning session at 36,930 yen, up 2,670 yen from the previous day. Tokyo Electron (8035.T) followed with a contribution of 283.17 points, SoftBank Group (9984.T) added 171.52 points, Fast Retailing (9983.T) contributed 137.54 points, and Ibiden (4062.T) added 105.18 points.

On the negative side, Tokio Marine Holdings (8766.T) was the largest drag, subtracting 13.65 points. Chugai Pharmaceutical (4519.T) followed at 13.05 points, Mitsubishi Corporation (8058.T) at 6.88 points, Otsuka Holdings (4578.T) at 6.57 points, and Recruit Holdings (6098.T) at 5.56 points.

The combined contribution of the top five positive contributors totaled 1,345.46 points, accounting for roughly 84% of the overall gain (1,602.09 points), while the top five negative contributors combined for only 45.71 points.

Nikkei Stock Average Firms in Afternoon Session, Supported by Asian Equity Gains and Rising U.S. Futures
sum: The Nikkei Stock Average firmed in the afternoon session on the 3rd on the Tokyo Stock Exchange, trading around the 64,500 level, up roughly 200 points from the previous day. Stock indices across Asian countries and regions were broadly firm, with South Korea's composite stock price index (KOSPI) and the Taiwan Weighted Index both rising, providing a tailwind for Japanese equities. Rising U.S. stock index futures in afternoon trading Japan time on the 3rd also underpinned the market.

The morning session had ended with a modest rebound. The Nikkei Stock Average closed the morning session at 64,455.83, up 130.19 points, on estimated trading volume of 945.73 million shares. The index opened at 64,724.81, up 399.17 points from the previous trading day, starting with a rebound. Supported by gains across the three major U.S. indices, an autonomous recovery from the previous day's sharp decline led the early going. However, buying failed to sustain, and the index narrowed its gains. Even as crude oil prices struggled to gain traction, uncertainty over the Middle East situation persisted, and selling on rallies capped the upside. Toward the morning close, the index traded in a range around the 64,400 level, ending the morning session with a modest gain.

The U.S. stock market rebounded on the 2nd, the previous day. The Dow Jones Industrial Average closed at 53,061.95, up 295.07 points, while the Nasdaq finished at 26,217.83, up 118.05 points. The market was mixed after the open as employment-related indicators came in weak, but Federal Reserve Bank of New York President John Williams said recent inflation data was "encouraging" and expressed the view that inflation is on a gradual downward trend as some tariff effects become a thing of the past, which pushed long-term interest rates lower. Tech stocks led the advance, and the market remained firm throughout the day.

President Williams also indicated that interest rates were at "an appropriate level" as of the conclusion of the previous Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The market interpreted this as a sign that the Fed is in no hurry to raise rates, contributing to dollar selling.

items.t: Nikkei Stock Average Falls 200 Yen as Rising Rates and Middle East Tensions Weigh, Semiconductors Provide Support
sum: The Nikkei Stock Average fell on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on the 21st, closing down 200.43 yen (0.30%) at 66,016.36. Rising long-term interest rates in Japan and the U.S., along with caution over the Middle East situation, weighed on the market, with selling spreading across heavyweight blue-chip stocks. The morning session saw losses exceed 900 yen at one point, but after selling ran its course, buybacks emerged in select artificial intelligence (AI) and semiconductor-related names, helping the index pare its losses.

In morning trading, the index stood at 66,008.45 at the midday break, down 208.34 yen (0.31%) from the previous close. The renewed rise in Japanese and U.S. long-term interest rates heightened awareness of the relative overvaluation of equities, putting selling pressure primarily on growth stocks. Additionally, geopolitical risks in the Middle East cooled investor sentiment, strengthening risk-averse positioning.

Among individual stocks, Fast Retailing, which has a large contribution to the Nikkei Stock Average, posted a sharp decline and became a major factor dragging down the index. The company's shares are known as one of the highest-priced constituents in the Nikkei, meaning a single stock exerts outsized influence on the overall index. The decline in Fast Retailing shares was one factor that briefly expanded the Nikkei's losses to over 900 yen.

Meanwhile, in afternoon trading, buybacks emerged in select AI and semiconductor-related names, partly supported by gains in the South Korean stock market. In addition to persistent expectations for expanding global semiconductor demand, the perception that valuations had become attractive following declines through the previous day appeared to invite bargain hunting. This helped the Nikkei narrow its losses, and the index maintained the 66,000 level into the close.

Among market participants, the trajectory of Japanese and U.S. long-term interest rates remains the primary focus. When rates rise, the discount rate used to calculate the present value of future earnings increases, creating headwinds particularly for high-valuation growth stocks.

items.t: Marketplace Mastery: Shein Breaks the $40 Billion Barrier in Europe and the US
sum: Europe’s influence in the Asian ultra-fast fashion giant’s business is on the rise, alongside the service division’s growth. In 2025, Shein reported revenues of $41.847 billion, marking an 8% increase.

Shein reveals some of its cards. The Chinese ultra fast fashion company, a major disruptor in the sector in recent years, has released details of its financial statements for the first time, revealing how Europe and the United States—along with its marketplace business—have propelled the group to exceed €40 billion in revenue for the first time in 2025.
Specifically, the company achieved global revenue of $41.847 billion in 2025, representing an 8% increase compared to the previous year, but a 20.7% increase over 2023.

Although it was widely expected, the draft IPO prospectus that the group has submitted to the Hong Kong Securities and Futures Commission reveals that Europe and the United States are the group’s largest markets. Specifically, Europe generated 35.4% of the group’s global revenue last year, with sales of $14,802 million in 2025. The continent’s share has been on the rise, up from 31.8% in 2023 and 35.1% in 2024.
Shein has maintained its U.S. business at around $10 billion over the past three years

Meanwhile, the U.S. business has remained at around $10 billion over the past three years, though its share has been declining. While the U.S. accounted for 29.4% of Shein’s sales in 2023, its share fell to 27% in 2024 and 24.1% in 2025, with a sales volume of $10,101 million.
With a presence in nearly 160 countries, Shein generated revenue of $16.944 billion in the rest of the world in 2025, accounting for the remaining 40.5%.

items.t: Nikkei 225 Plunges 2,884 Yen as China's Chip Equipment Push Triggers Sell-Off in High-Priced Tech Stocks; KOSPI Crash Adds Fuel to the Fire
sum: The Nikkei 225 suffered a sharp reversal on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on July 28, ending the morning session down 2,884.73 points (4.44%) at 62,046.46. The decline briefly exceeded 3,000 points, pushing the index below the psychologically important 62,000 level. The sell-off was triggered by reports that a Chinese state-backed enterprise has commenced manufacturing of immersion deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography equipment, sparking a rush to dump high-priced semiconductor equipment stocks. The plunge in South Korea's KOSPI, which triggered a circuit breaker, further chilled investor sentiment and prompted overseas speculators to sell Nikkei 225 futures.

In the U.S. market on July 27, the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX), which tracks major chip-related stocks, fell more than 2%. Semiconductor equipment makers were sold on intensifying concerns over competition from Chinese firms, and the Nasdaq closed down 43.74 points at 24,932.08. Carrying that momentum into Tokyo, semiconductor-related names fell across the board from the opening bell. Heavyweight index contributors such as Advantest (6857.T), Tokyo Electron (8035.T), Lasertec (6920.T), and Disco (6146.T) all tumbled sharply, dragging the Nikkei lower.

Advantest was the biggest drag on the index, followed by Tokyo Electron. Major memory chipmaker Kioxia Holdings (285A.T) breached the ¥50,000 (approximately $305) threshold and was at one point sold down to its daily limit.

A buildup of margin trading long positions also accelerated the decline. According to the Nikkei, Kioxia's margin ratio stood at 36 times as of July 17, with long positions vastly exceeding short positions. SoftBank Group (9984.T) similarly had a large overhang of margin longs. Shigetoshi Kamata, senior advisor at Tachibana Securities, noted that "many individual investors who had bought Kioxia and SoftBank Group on margin were forced to sell at a loss."

Turmoil in the South Korean market added fuel to the fire. The Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) plunged more than 9% from the previous day on July 28, triggering a circuit breaker that temporarily halted trading. The violent swing prompted a surge in Nikkei 225 futures selling by overseas speculators.

Fast Retailing’s Climate Gains Start With Its Supply Chain
sum: Fast Retailing is stepping up its climate ambition—and it has its supply chain to thank for it.

After slashing its Scope 3 carbon emissions by 20 percent from a 2019 baseline and hitting its target five years ahead of schedule, the Uniqlo parent company has raised the stakes, aiming for an additional 10 percent reduction by 2030.

“Initially, we wanted to be careful about what we were committing to,” Kazumi Yanai, director at Fast Retailing, said at a sustainability discussion at the Uniqlo showroom in New York City on Thursday. “Then because we saw progress, we raised the bar.”

Scope 3 emissions, which encompass all indirect greenhouse gases across a company’s value chain, are notoriously difficult to measure and manage because they originate with suppliers or consumers. At the same time, they often make up at least 75 percent of the total climate impact.

Case in point: Fast Retailing shrank its Scope 1 and 2 emissions, which are within its direct control, by 90.3 percent by 2025, five years earlier than planned, by increasing the share of renewable energy in its stores and offices to 93.5 percent, up from 84.7 percent in 2024.

A driver of the company’s brisk Scope 3 performance has been its pivot to less polluting raw materials, which now account for 19.4 percent of its total mix and are expected to reach 50 percent by 2030. Recycled polyester from PET bottles, in particular, constitutes 46.4 percent of all polyester used, up from 41.5 percent a year ago.

Still, Fast Retailing ultimately credits its deep-rooted supplier relationships as the true engine of its progress. Many of those partnerships, Yanai said, have lasted decades—an anomaly in an industry where a “race to the bottom,” as Cascale editorial director Kaley Roshitsh put it, encourages supplier hopping in search of the lowest price per unit.

Puig’s Stock Takes a 13% Dive While Estée Lauder Surges Following Failed Merger
sum: Following a breakdown in discussions with Estée Lauder, the Spanish company’s stock took a double-digit dive. In contrast, the American giant experienced a 10.02% uptick in pre-market Wall Street activity.

Puig shares are down 13.49% at mid-session today, to €15.23 per share, after it was announced yesterday, at the close of the market, that the Spanish firm and Estée Lauder had decided to end the talks they were holding to carry out a potential merger of their respective businesses, without reaching an agreement.

Its collapse on the stock market contrasts with the rebound that the U.S. firm’s shares are experiencing in the pre-opening of Wall Street, which have risen up to 10.02% after finishing yesterday’s trading day, when the news was not yet known, with an increase of 0.91%.
Since the possible merger talks came to light last March, Puig’s shares had risen 17.37% until yesterday, while those of Estée Lauder fell 8.16%.
“We value the enriching conversations that have been held with The Estée Lauder Companies,“ said Puig’s CEO

Yesterday the two companies announced that they were breaking off merger talks. “The parties have terminated talks on a possible business merger,“ Estée Lauder said in a statement. Puig, for its part, has pronounced itself in the same sense, stressing that “the companies have not reached an agreement for a potential merger of their respective businesses”.

Although the official reasons for the breakdown of the talks have not transcended, during the last few days it has been known that one of the stumbling blocks could have been the position of the founder of Charlotte Tilbury, a brand owned by Puig.

items.t: Victoria’s Secret Unveils New Era with Ticker Change to VSXY on the Stock Market
sum: The intimate apparel brand, after triumphantly navigating a challenging financial storm in recent years, is doubling down on its signature allure that both defined its identity and led to its downfall: sexiness.

Victoria’s Secret has decided to show off what is so characteristic of it and which, at the same time, was one of the causes of its crises, even on the stock market. The U.S. company opens a new chapter in its history with the change of its ticker to VSXY on the New York Stock Exchange as of June 2nd.

After years of growth, Victoria’s Secret began in 2017 to weaken as it became disconnected from its consumers, who no longer wanted the ideal of sexy that the brand represented nor its iconic fashion shows. In 2021, Victoria’s Secret even became a standalone company, following L Brands’ decision to separate the intimate brand from its perfume and cosmetics business, Bath&Body Works.

After canceling its runway show and modifying its communication to be more inclusive, in 2024 Victoria’s Secret broke new ground with the addition of Hillary Super as CEO. The executive came from SavagexFenti, one of the intimate apparel brands that stole the market from Victoria’s Secret with a proposal more in line with the new aesthetic canons and consumer styles.
Victoria’s Secret has faced in recent weeks a shareholder against the management team’s management

Having regained some of its lost ground, Victoria’s Secret now wants to reclaim a key element of its brand: sexy. “Sexy has always been part of our DNA; what has changed is the determination with which we reclaim it: not by telling women what sexy should look like, but by reflecting it to them in a way that is authentic, broad and modern,“ Super said in a statement.

“VSXY is a recognizable brand and is in line with our strategy and the progress we have made; it reflects our conviction and confidence in this work; we embrace who we are and are proud of it,“ he added.

Lemaire’s quiet luxury is making waves, from Paris to Shanghai
sum: The French fashion house redefines everyday elegance with globally influential designs, epitomised by the unique Croissant bag

There is a specific “Lemaire person” currently walking the pavements of Paris. From his studio window near a university, Christophe Lemaire sees them pass every morning: academics in crisp poplin, and creatives in oversized blousons and balloon-legged denim with the inevitable crescent-shaped bag slung across their chest.
“It may not even be Lemaire they are wearing,” the eponymous designer notes with quiet pride, “but you can feel the style is influenced by us. That is very gratifying.”

This speaks to the success of the independent French label co-helmed by Lemaire and Sarah-Linh Tran – as well as its paradox. For a label that shuns the traditional levers of fashion business, releasing collections that prioritise consistent DNA over newness, Lemaire has become remarkably, even reluctantly, ubiquitous.

There have been growing pains: the label recently met friction in China, when a campaign for its new Objets Senteur line was withdrawn from social media after users drew links to forced queue-cutting during the Qing dynasty, prompting the brand to publish an apology. Nonetheless, in an industry obsessed with “quiet luxury”, the designers have managed to achieve a genuinely influential vernacular.

The numbers back this up. Just over five years after Uniqlo owner Fast Retailing bought a minority share of the business in 2018 (the duo already led the brand’s R&D centre and designed Uniqlo’s popular U range), Lemaire’s sales exceeded €100 million (around US$116 million) in 2024, according to Business of Fashion. Yet, true to their media-shy reputation, the designers are less interested in the balance sheet and more in what they call the “dialectic”.

Fast Retailing stock fell 1.35 percent on October 2 as sales rose 10.8 percent
sum: Fast Retailing stock (ISIN JP3802300008) closed at JPY 71,770 on the Tokyo Stock Exchange on October 2, down 1.35 percent from JPY 72,750. The move followed a stronger September sales update from UNIQLO Japan, although the market still faces a fresh test when the retailer reports fiscal 2026 results.

According to MarketScreener on October 2, UNIQLO Japan same-store sales including online sales rose 10.8 percent year over year in September 2026. Total sales including online sales increased 9.9 percent, giving the domestic business a clear improvement after weaker summer comparisons.

The mix matters because customer numbers fell 0.5 percent, while average purchase per customer increased 11.3 percent, according to MarketScreener. The September result therefore points more toward higher spending per shopper than broader customer traffic, with cooler temperatures and fall-winter products supporting demand.

Fast Retailing's market capitalization stood at JPY 22.0 trillion on October 2, with trading volume of 1,188,700 shares. The stock remained 19.1 percent below its 52-week high of JPY 88,690, but it was 54.4 percent above the 52-week low of JPY 46,490.

The October 2 session opened at JPY 72,180 and reached an intraday high of JPY 72,290 before falling to a low of JPY 70,960. That range shows that the 1.35 percent decline was not a single-price anomaly, but a full-session move below the prior close.

Fast Retailing's investor-relations calendar lists October 8, 2026, for the announcement of fiscal 2026 business results, according to the company's IR calendar. The date follows the September sales release and will determine whether domestic momentum translated into group-level earnings progress.

For the earnings release, the key distinction is between volume and pricing. September same-store sales rose 10.8 percent while customer numbers declined 0.5 percent, so investors will have to assess whether average purchase growth of 11.3 percent can persist across UNIQLO Japan and the international businesses.

Fast Retailing shares soar to record high after the Uniqlo owner lifts profit forecast
sum: Fast Retailing shares surged more than 9% to a record high on Friday after the Japanese parent of Uniqlo lifted its annual outlook and as robust international growth boosted its quarterly profit.

Reflecting the stronger first-half performance and favorable currency assumptions, the company raised its full-year outlook for operating profit to 700 billion yen ($4.4 billion) from 650 billion yen forecast earlier.
The company sees a prolonged runway for expansion, with CEO Tadashi Yanai signaling "significant growth ahead" in a presentation on Thursday.

Fast Retailing reported a strong set of interim results for the six months ended Feb. 28, 2026, with revenue rising 14.8% year on year to 2.06 trillion yen and operating profit jumping 31.7% to 400.6 billion yen, as robust global demand for Uniqlo drove broad-based growth across regions.

Performance was led by Uniqlo International, where revenue surged 22.4% and profit rose 37.4%, supported by strong sales across Greater China, Southeast Asia, and Western markets, alongside continued traction in year-round apparel, the company said in its earnings release.

The retailer, however, acknowledged that the Middle East conflict was beginning to feed into costs, particularly through higher transportation expenses in some markets, adding that earlier adjustments to production and logistics have helped cushion supply chain risks. "This will not have a major impact from a production and distribution perspective," the company said.
Fast Retailing's portfolio of brands includes Uniqlo, GU, Theory, Comptoir des Cotonniers and PLST.

Cotton On Isn’t Closing. How Are Other Fashion Brands Faring?
sum: Yesterday, the internet exploded. Headlines screamed that Cotton On, a brand that’s been a staple of Singapore’s retail scene for nearly 20 years, was liquidating and closing all 30+ stores.

For many Singaporeans, Cotton On is that go-to shop at the mall. Affordable tees, basic essentials, a quick grab on your way out. So when news broke that Cotton On Asia Pte. Ltd. had entered voluntary liquidation via a Government Gazette notice, it hit a nerve.
Cotton On came out and said: we’re not closing. The stores will stay open.
There are two entities: Cotton On Asia Pte. Ltd. and Cotton On Singapore Pte. Ltd.

Cotton On Asia is the holding company. It doesn’t operate any stores. It doesn’t employ any staff. It was essentially a dormant corporate shell that was no longer needed as part of their group structure.
Cotton On Singapore, on the other hand, is the entity that actually runs the 30+ stores here. And on ACRA’s Bizfile, that entity is still very much “live.”

So the Government Gazette notice? It was about liquidating a holding company, not shutting down your neighbourhood Cotton On. The management clarified that this was a routine corporate restructuring and that they have no plans to exit Asia.

items.t: Interview with the CEO
sum: Fast Retailing has always pursued business based on its mission to make the world a better place through clothes. I am a firm believer that everyone across the world has a right to wear clothes that have been carefully designed and carefully produced using high-quality materials. I call this the democratization of clothing.

Until UNIQLO came on the scene, clothing items made from great materials that offered high functionality and sophisticated designs were exclusive and expensive. We opened up this clothing to everyone. Today, we offer sophisticated simplicity in the design of high-quality, comfortable and carefully crafted clothes at affordable prices. My hope is that by changing clothes, we can change everyday life and ultimately change the world. LifeWear has made that hope achievable.

Growing global support for LifeWear is creating something of a worldwide UNIQLO boom. UNIQLO rose to No. 47 in the Best Global Brands 2025,* its highest ranking ever, and Fast Retailing and UNIQLO have been widely covered in mainstream media around the world, including 'The New York Times' and 'The New Yorker' in the USA, and 'The Times' in the UK. This is testament to the growing global customer support for LifeWear and to the infinite possibilities of LifeWear itself.
* Published by the leading global branding consultancy, Interbrand

Our stores are extremely effective at conveying the value of LifeWear to customers. Communication with customers in our roughly 3,500 stores is the source of all sorts of information and the foundation of our business. Our global store network is our greatest strength. We exceed our customers' expectations by offering optimal product lineups, colors, and sizes at each store based on local needs. Our strategy is to create genuinely meaningful stores that offer enjoyable shopping experiences and useful services for all customers.

One such store is UNIQLO Meir, which was opened in Antwerp, Belgium in September 2025. UNIQLO designs complement the exquisite 16th-century interior of this elegant flagship, creating a perfect blend of traditional and modern. Thanks to community collaborations, local customers immediately feel at home.

The proposed bilateral trade agreement between India and the U.S. has yet to be finalised, despite six rounds of negotiations since March. U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick claimed on the All-In Podcast that the deal stalled because Prime Minister Narendra Modi did not call Donald Trump. The Trump administration has already imposed 50% tariffs on India, including 25% linked to India’s purchases of Russian oil, among the highest levied on any country. India has described the U.S. action as “unfair, unjustified and unreasonable”.

The uncertainty has intensified ahead of a U.S. Supreme Court ruling on the legality of Trump’s tariffs. If deemed “illegal”, the U.S. government could be forced to refund nearly $150 billion to importers, a decision that could significantly alter the global trade landscape.

After the sharp correction yesterday triggered by the possibility of about 500% tariff on India under the provisions of the Russia Sanctioning Act approved by President Trump, the market will be focused on the verdict expected today from the US Supreme Court on the legality of Trump tariffs, said Dr. VK Vijayakumar, Chief Investment Strategist at Geojit Investments.

"There is a high probability of the verdict going against Trump. But the details are significant: that is, whether it would be a partial striking down of the tariffs or completely declaring the tariffs illegal. The market reaction would depend on the details. If the Supreme Court declares Trump tariffs illegal, there would be a rally in India since India has been the worst affected by the 50% tariffs," said Vijayakumar.

sum: Japanese shares linked to the tourism industry have nosedived following China’s warning to its citizens against travelling to Japan.

Relations between Tokyo and Beijing have plummeted since Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi suggested earlier this month that Japan’s military could intervene to stop China from taking control of Taiwan.

In a sharp escalation of the dispute on Friday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs advised citizens to avoid travel to the East Asian country, claiming that Takaichi’s comments had increased risks to their “personal safety and lives”.
The issue continued to reverberate as Japan’s stock market reopened on Monday after the weekend break, with shares of airlines and retail outlets taking sharp falls.
Department store group Isetan Mitsukoshi fell more than 11 percent in afternoon trading, while its rival Takashimaya tumbled about 5 percent.
Japan Airlines fell about 4 percent, while Uniqlo owner Fast Retailing dipped about 5 percent. Cosmetics company Shiseido plunged about 9.5 percent.

China is Japan’s biggest source of foreign tourists, accounting for almost one-quarter of the 31.65 million arrivals in the first nine months of this year, according to the Japan National Tourism Organization.

items.t: Japan's tourism shares slump as diplomatic rift with China worsens
China travel warning for Japan sends shares in tourism and retail companies plunging
sum: Shares in Japanese tourism and retail firms have fallen sharply after China warned its citizens not to travel to Japan, while a senior Japanese diplomat was due to travel to Beijing amid an escalating row over comments about Taiwan made by the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi.

Relations between the two countries have deteriorated dramatically in the past week after Takaichi, a conservative who has hawkish views on China, suggested that Japanese self-defence forces could intervene if a Chinese attempt to invade Taiwan represented a “survival-threatening situation” for Japan.

The comments – a reflection of the views of politicians on the right of Takaichi’s Liberal Democratic party – triggered a furious response from Beijing, including calls for Chinese citizens to boycott Japan as a tourist destination, and a coastguard sail-by through the disputed Senkaku islands at the weekend.

In an attempt to prevent tensions from escalating, Masaaki Kanai, the director general of the Japanese foreign ministry’s Asia and Oceania bureau, will meet his Chinese counterpart, Liu Jinsong, on Tuesday, Japanese media reported.
Kanai is expected to reassure Liu that Takaichi’s comments do not signal a shift in Japanese security policy, and to urge China to refrain from actions that could damage bilateral ties.
The call by Beijing for Chinese travellers to avoid Japan – which was followed by advice that students reconsider taking up places at Japanese universities – is already affecting businesses.

In morning trade on Monday, shares in the Japanese cosmetics firm Shiseido fell 9%, in department store group Takashimaya by more than 5% and in Fast Retailing – the owner of the Uniqlo clothing brand – by more than 4%.
